text: Everything from the scoped checklist through the runbook exists to support one fifteen-minute conversation with Dale. That conversation is where this project either lands as something he trusts, or as a pile of technical work he can't evaluate.

The biggest mistake in presenting security work is walking through every setting changed on every server before saying what it means. Dale doesn't need a line-by-line account of sshd_config. Mara opens with the headline: your four servers are hardened to an industry-standard checklist, and we have a working alert that would have caught someone actually using a phished password -- the exact scenario from two weeks ago.

Only after that does the walkthrough move to supporting detail -- the headline in fifteen seconds, the how in a minute or two at a level Dale can actually evaluate, and then the proof, live, for the remaining time.

Describing a detection rule is far less convincing than watching it work. Mara re-runs one of last lesson's test scenarios live in Sentinel -- the one that should fire -- and shows the alert appear. Then she runs the one that shouldn't fire, and shows it correctly produces nothing. Seeing both does more to build trust than any slide, because it answers the question every manager has: is this going to bury my team in false alarms?

Dale doesn't need to understand join kind equals inner to trust the result. Mara translates: the rule looks for someone guessing wrong several times and then getting it right. We tested it against a normal typo and confirmed it stays quiet. And everything is written down, so this isn't something only I can maintain -- directly answering what Dale actually asked for back in lesson one.
With the findings presented, next lesson handles the one pushback question Dale raises before signing off.
